# Issues

**The register of everything open in this repo.** Defects, gaps, and questions
awaiting a ruling. One id per item, stable forever.

**This file is the source of truth for what is open.** Nothing is open unless it
is here. Other documents no longer carry their own open-item lists — they link
here. Long analysis may stay where it was argued (`packages/*/PROJECT_STATE.md`,
`IDEAS/*.md`); the **Detail** column points at it. What must
never happen again is an item existing in exactly one document that nobody reads.

**What belongs here:** shipped behavior that is wrong, a gap that blocks
something, a question that needs a decision. **What does not:** features and
roadmap (`IDEAS/`), settled rulings (`DECISIONS.md`), traps that are correct
behavior you must know about (`CLAUDE.md` § Live hazards), history
(git, `FJS-D675`).

**Closed items age out to [ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md).**
§ Closed below keeps the recent ones; the archive keeps the rest, verbatim.
Together they hold every id ever issued, and an id is never reused — so a
`FJS-###` named in a comment, a handoff, or a package file resolves in exactly
one of the two files. Search both before concluding an id is unknown.

## Conventions

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Id** | `FJS-###` for a defect or gap, `FJS-D##` for a decision. **Never reused, never renumbered.** Closing an item moves it to § Closed with its id. |
| **Sev** | `S1` blocker — data loss, a security hole, or cannot ship · `S2` high — silently wrong, costs a day to find · `S3` medium · `S4` low or cosmetic |
| **Status** | `open` — verified open on the date shown · `stale?` — inherited from an older audit and **not re-verified**; probe before acting · `contested` — the recorded diagnosis is doubted, see the note |
| **Verified** | The date somebody last ran it. A `stale?` row's date is when it was *written*, not confirmed. |
| **Blocked by** | A row that cannot start until another closes says `blocked by FJS-###` in its own text, and nowhere else. `fli next` takes it out of the ranking until that row closes and weighs the blocker up. Write it only where the order is real — a row that merely relates to another cites it. |
| **By hand** | A row a headless session cannot finish — a run longer than a session lasts, a check only the owner can make — says `by hand` as its own segment of its links cell. `fli next` keeps it ranked and marks it; `fix:loop` skips it. |
| **Env** | A row whose fix is the environment and not the code says `env: <cause>` as its own segment of its links cell, cause one of `port` · `shared db` · `stale process` · `timing` · `real machine` · `network` (`FJS-D1118`). The segment names where the FIX lives, not where the symptom shows. `fli next` keeps it ranked and marks it; `fix:loop` skips it; `fli register:check` refuses a cause outside the list (`env-cause`) and warns on a title that reads like one with no segment (`env-smell`). |
| **Seam** | A row whose bug crosses a named handoff says `seam: <name>` as its own segment of its links cell, the name from the root `CLAUDE.md` § Bridge index key list (`FJS-D1135`). `env:` names where the fix lives; `seam:` names which handoff the bug crosses. Written by hand; `fli register:check` refuses a name the key list does not hold (`seam-name`). |

**A row has exactly the columns its table's header names**, and `fli
register:check` fails on anything else (`row-shape`). Both ways of getting it
wrong are silent: a row with FEWER columns is one pasted from the other table,
and the reader infers a shape from the cell count, so it is given a status
nobody wrote and no other rule can see it; a row with MORE has the excess
**dropped when the file is rendered** — in § Closed that is the *How* column, so
the row displays with no citations while they sit in the file. Links belong
inside the last declared column, joined with ` · `, and a `|` that is part of a
sentence is escaped `\|`.

`stale?` is load-bearing. The eight rows inherited from the 2026-07-31 audit
(now `IDEAS/review-coherence.md`) were re-probed on 2026-08-10 and **five of the eight were wrong**:
two were already fixed (conduit's secrets, `admin:generate`), one was never
reproducible (conduit's version skew), and two were right about a defect and
wrong about what it was — sierra's prefetch is not an auth *bypass* but a
cached 401, and caravan's row named three bugs of which two were fixed.
**Treat a `stale?` row as a lead, not a fact** (`VERIFYING.md`).

**The register also goes stale in the closing direction, which nothing here was
watching for.** `FJS-043` was fixed in the tree with a comment describing the
old defect in the past tense, and stayed `open` for eight days because closing
is a second action nobody owed. A row's `Verified` date is evidence about when
somebody last *looked*, not about whether the defect survives — 22 rows carried
`open` at 2026-08-02 when this audit ran, which is the same fiction `stale?`
exists to name, wearing the other label.

| <a id="fjs-3093"></a>FJS-3093 | junction | **A raw route cannot stream its body: _handleRequest parses and buffers every matched route's body before the handler runs and $raw.$req is rebuilt from the kept bytes, so an upload larger than memory has to leave junction for a second Bun.serve** | open | 2026-10-16 | immich stressor Q1, 2026-10-16. http.ts ~749 calls parseBody(req, maxBodySize) for every matched route — services, plugin routes, app.post() alike — and the handler's $raw.$req is a new Request over parsed.bytes. No route option says 'hand me the stream', so a chunked or resumable upload endpoint cannot be a junction route at any size: the bytes are one ArrayBuffer (then a second copy in parseMultipart's slice, then a File) before the app sees them. The app's answer is api/src/core/upload.ts, a second Bun.serve on PORT+2 streaming req.body to disk with createWriteStream + drain backpressure and sha256 on the way: 1 GB in 7.0 s, RSS 86 → 144 MB peak, settled 92 MB; four 1 GB uploads at once in 20.3 s, RSS peak 178 MB, every stored file hashing to its source. Outpost's second listener (FJS-D345) is the same move. RULING OWED (PLAN.md § Q1 writes A/B/C): whether the stream belongs to a route-level body contract in junction, to FileStorage as a mounted upload protocol, or outside the API as direct-to-provider. · Ruled 2026-10-16: the fix is a route-level `{ body: 'stream' }` that skips parseBody, FJS-D1159 |
| <a id="fjs-3092"></a>FJS-3092 | junction | **A multipart file part above 50 MB is dropped in silence: MAX_FILE_SIZE in body.ts is a module constant no option reaches, the write reaches the service without the field, and the transport answers neither 413 nor 422** | open | 2026-10-16 | immich stressor, 2026-10-16. With maxBodySize raised to 2 GiB, a 60 MB and a 100 MB multipart upload (one file part) answer 200-shaped: parseMultipart pushes a part only when content.byteLength <= maxFileSize (body.ts ~513), so the part is skipped, files is [], and the service's $.data has no file — the app's own 422 was the only refusal. A create into a required File column would 400 on 'missing field' about a field the caller sent. No option names the cap (parseBody takes maxBodySize only), so an app that needs 51 MB cannot ask for it. Measured on PORT=7270; a 40 MB part lands, a 60 MB one vanishes. |

| <a id="fjs-257"></a>FJS-257 | basecamp · outpost | **The Outpost exists and has never run on a real machine.** Was *a deploy with no Outpost reports six green steps and runs nothing*, and the scope has narrowed twice since. Basecamp's half closed 2026-08-19 — `providers/executor.ts` answers outpost / named stub / refusal, `apps.place` writes the placement three jobs read and nothing wrote, and a digest the machine reports is recorded on `Deployment.builtImage` and addressed by every later step. `packages/outpost` is the process on the other end: the route table basecamp already spoke, every route but liveness signed, build-on-target answering the digest of what it built, and a heartbeat that registers the machine as a Conduit target. basecamp's drive runs the REAL server with a fake docker runner, so the protocol both sides speak is graded rather than restated. **Three clauses of this row went false on 2026-09-08 and are struck**: *nothing installs an Outpost on a server* (cloud-init installs one on a machine basecamp bought, and `servers.issueEnrollment` prints the one command that installs one on a machine somebody else made — `docs/PROVISIONING.md` P2/P5), *there is no `pending → provisioning → installing → ready` walk* (the walk is declared on `@@transitions` and driven end to end by `verify:provision`; `ready` was deleted by [FJS-1021](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1021) and `installing` is what a first heartbeat leaves), and *the fleet shares one secret, so a compromised machine can forge another's check-in* (every machine holds a credential minted at enrollment, inbound and outbound both resolve it per machine, and `OUTPOST_SECRET` is not declared any more — P3/P5). **What remains is one claim, and it is now bigger than the row that carried it**: nothing here has run against a real machine. **The Docker-daemon clause is struck** (2026-09-26): `packages/outpost/test/docker-live.test.js` grades the inspector against a real daemon's own byte counts, read off its API socket, and the first meeting found both of the inspector's readings wrong — Docker's human sizes are decimal and were scaled by 1024, so every disk report read 2–7% fuller than the disk, and `volume prune` takes no `--format`, so the unused-volume sweep exited 125 having removed nothing. That grade covers `system df` and `volume prune`; `build`, `run` and `logs` still meet a daemon first on a fleet machine. **What stays open is the box**: the cloud-init script — the Docker install, the Bun install, the systemd unit and the enrollment exchange — has only ever been `sh -n`-parsed. It is this repo's reading of a vendor's documentation, which is the same limit `verify:stripe` names, and the only thing that closes it is a real account and a real box. Build-once-promote-a-digest is still §b for basecamp and the Outpost: V1 builds on the target, which is honest while the Outpost is co-resident with basecamp and stops being honest at the second machine. **The CLI half of digest addressing is not open and the clause saying so is struck** (2026-09-13): `04-build-api` asks the built image what it is and `06-swap` starts `imageAddress`, falling back to the tag only when the inspect fails | open | 2026-10-16 | [packages/outpost](packages/outpost/) · [executor.ts](packages/basecamp/api/src/providers/executor.ts) · [enrollment.ts](packages/basecamp/api/src/providers/compute/enrollment.ts) · [PROVISIONING.md](packages/basecamp/docs/PROVISIONING.md) · [IDEAS/deploy-plane.md](IDEAS/deploy-plane.md) · by hand · blocked by `FJS-1397` · env: real machine |

So on a model that declares both, a named move is reachable only by asSystem(), which lifts the move's @gate — the one thing @version should not change. Workaround in etsy (api/src/services/shops.service.ts): spell the move as `update({ data: { status: 'suspended', version: row.version } })`, which litestone identifies as the same move by its (from, to) pair and grades the same. | <a id="fjs-3081"></a>FJS-3081 | caravan | **cancel() of a running job marks the row cancelled while the handler's process tree is alive — ctx.signal reaches the handler and nothing a handler is handed reaches a child's children, so a job that spawned sh -c leaks its grandchildren with the row saying cancelled** | open | 2026-10-16 | Measured in the ci-runner stressor (fjs-prototypes/ci-runner PLAN.md 0.3), standalone createCaravan over a scratch jobs.db, pollInterval 200, three handlers each spawning sh -c 'sleep 120 & sleep 120 & wait' (one shell, two grandchildren), then cancel(id) while running. (1) handler ignores ctx.signal: cancel() returns true, row.status is cancelled at once, abort fired in the handler after 1ms, and 500ms later the shell AND both grandchildren are alive. (2) handler does child.kill('SIGTERM') on abort: the shell dies, both grandchildren survive reparented to init — the shell is what spawn() returns and a signal to it stops at it. (3) handler spawns with detached:true and does process.kill(-pgid,'SIGTERM') on abort: the group is empty 500ms later. So the row's word is true only for a handler that spawned into its own process group and kills the group, and nothing in JobContext, caravan's docs or the CLAUDE.md says so — the hazard list stops at 'a handler that ignores it keeps running'. Phase 1 of the same stressor built the group version (api/src/core/runner.ts: detached spawn, SIGTERM -pgid, grace, SIGKILL -pgid, sweep on exit) and measured it over two API instances on one jobs.db against a 10-process tree with a SIGTERM trapper: same-instance abort after 5–6ms, cross-instance after 288–511ms (4 samples, bound pollInterval 1000ms), every tree empty by ps afterwards. What the group kill cannot reach is a child that left the group (setsid sleep 300 survived; a cgroup is the answer there). This is a ruling wearing a bug report: whether Caravan hands a handler a child-process helper (spawn in own group, kill group on abort, sweep on exit) or stays signal-only and documents that a handler that spawns owns its process group. Options are written in ci-runner/PLAN.md § Q1. |

Tag { name String; slug String @slug @default(name) @unique }. sys.tag.create({ data: { name: 'Probe Tag One' } }) answers slug 'probe-tag-one'. sys.tag.createMany({ data: [{ name: 'Probe Tag Two' }] }) throws SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_NOTNULL 'tag.slug' (client.js writeUnit ~5912). createMany({ data: [{ name: 'Probe Tag Three', slug: 'Probe Tag Three' }] }) stores 'probe-tag-three', so the transform half of the attribute runs in bulk and the sibling-copy half of @default does not — the one path a 1,000-row seed takes is the one path where the schema's default is dead. The three: Service Autopilot's day window; 3CX GetCallLogData polled every 5 min from lastSyncAt minus a 10-min overlap, capped at 24 h, with a 04:00 3-day backstop, which still loses 84% of calls over 10 min by the reference's own study (window shape, not cadence); Graph's per-folder deltaLink, where a 410 means restart the round and @removed tombstones arrive in the same page. The brief refuses both shipped transports in one sentence — *if the reminder is an email nobody opens, or a badge inside an app that is not running, the person is late and we have paid for a system that did nothing* — so this product is the first on the list that is WRONG rather than lesser without push. **Ground state re-probed 2026-09-22:** `ls packages/notifications/drivers/` is `email.ts`, `inapp.ts`; `grep -rn 'vapid\|web-push' packages/ --include=*.ts --include=*.js` is **0 hits across the whole framework**. **What was free, and it is worth saying first.** The `transports:` seam cost nothing: anything with `send(recipient, message, app)` registers, a registered driver beats a built-in name, a transport with no driver is refused BEFORE any delivery rather than at the moment one is needed, and a `push:` formatter beside `inApp:` on a `defineNotification` needs no adapter. Nothing in the app is a workaround for this package. **What 2.17 and `ecosystem-gaps.md` § 16 both get wrong.** Both argue that making the subscription a Model *is the whole argument for building it here rather than leaving it to an app*, because it then inherits `@@gate`, `@encrypted` on the keys and Invariant 7's redaction, where *every hand-rolled version is a plain table with none of that*. **Measured: a hand-rolled version in a FrontierJS app is not a plain table.** `model PushSubscription` was declared in the app's own `db/schema.lite` and got all three — `@encrypted` hides `p256dh`/`authSecret` from every caller read and returns PLAINTEXT to `asSystem()`, which is what a sender needs and is the one of the five visibility words that fits; the audit trail carries `[redacted]` (see [FJS-1266](#fjs-1266) for the half of that which is a defect); and the gate is the app's to state. That argument is an argument for litestone, which the app already has. **What actually costs, measured.** `api/src/core/push.ts` is **~350 lines** implementing RFC 8291 (aes128gcm over ECDH-ES), RFC 8188 (the body framing) and RFC 8292 (VAPID): an ephemeral P-256 keypair per send, **four HKDF derivations** whose `info` strings must be byte-exact including their NULs, a `salt‖rs‖idlen‖keyid` header, the `0x02` last-record delimiter, and a JWT whose signature must be raw `r‖s` where node emits ASN.1 DER by default. **Every one of those fails the same way: the push service does not hold the key, cannot tell a bad derivation from a good one, and answers `201 Created`.** A wrong build is indistinguishable from a phone in a tunnel, which is why the app's own test decrypts what it encrypts with a device private key rather than asserting a length — every cheaper check passes on garbage. **Three more things an app must build that the driver interface does not suggest.** (1) **A driver that WRITES**: a subscription expires with no notice and the only signal is a 404/410 on a send, so the transport that delivers is the one that must prune; `transport`/`send`/`shutdown` hints at none of it. (2) **A fan-out inside the fan-out**: `inApp` writes one row per recipient, but a person is N devices with N key pairs and N independent 410s, and `Recipient` — whose design note is *a Recipient is not a User* — has nowhere to put them. (3) **`asSystem()` on every send**, because the keys are `@encrypted` and the sender reads everybody's rows, which is [FJS-1216](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1216)'s cost once more: every delivery is filed against the application rather than against anybody. **The boundary § 16 says to settle first, with a measurement.** *A push payload is a read that leaves the building via a vendor, so `@guarded` columns must not be in it.* It cannot be enforced at the driver: the driver necessarily holds `asSystem()` to decrypt the subscription keys at all, so it has full visibility by construction. The check belongs where the payload is BUILT — the notification's `push:` formatter — or nowhere. **Scope note:** measured to the edge, no vendor send, per that run's scope call. The request is built completely — URL, headers, VAPID JWT, encrypted body — and handed to an injected `deliver`; the default is a plain `fetch`, since a push service is ordinary HTTPS with no SDK and no account, which is what makes this buildable by an app at all. · `IDEAS/overview.md` 2.17 · `IDEAS/ecosystem-gaps.md` § 16 · [FJS-1270](#fjs-1270) · [FJS-1266](#fjs-1266) · [FJS-1234](#fjs-1234) · driven in `api/test/reminders.test.ts` |

| <a id="fjs-1246"></a>FJS-1246 | example | **`example`'s payroll has no input shape for a MEASURED hour: `annualGross` is `rate * hoursPerWeek * 52` and `hoursPerWeek` is an `Int` contracted constant, so a workforce product's whole output can reach a payslip only by being averaged back into the contract it was measured to replace.** | open | 2026-09-22 | **Graded, not ported** — PLAN.md § Q6 in the connectteam stressor, against the shapes `example/api/src/domain/payroll/` demands and with nothing copied into that tree. An approved timesheet (`@@transitions`, `@seals`, lines carrying `onDate`, `kind`, `minutes` and a `rateSnapshot` frozen at the rate in force on the day) was converted into `PayWindowRow` and run through transcribed copies of `annualGross` and `periodShare`. **It goes, and everything that makes it a measurement is lost on the way.** Spring fortnight: 420 measured minutes, **€84.00 actually earned**, → `{ basis: 'hourly', rate: 1200, hoursPerWeek: 4 }` → `annualGross` €2496.00 → `periodShare(·, 26)` **€96.00 — out by €12.00**. Autumn fortnight: 540 minutes, €108.00 earned → `hoursPerWeek: 5` → €3120.00 → **€120.00, out by €12.00**. **Four refusals, and only the fourth is one a type checker catches.** (1) `hoursPerWeek` is an `Int @gte(0) @lte(168)`, so a fortnight holding one 7-hour night is **3.5 h/week and is stored as 4** — the rounding alone is the whole €12.00. (2) `PayWindow` holds ONE `rate` for a window while a timesheet holds a `rateSnapshot` per LINE, so a raise mid-period is a fact about a day at one end and a fact about a window at the other, and neither shape can express the other without losing the split. (3) `PayComponentKind.overtime` is in `EARNING_KINDS` and `draftPayslip` emits exactly one earning line, always `basicPay`; `overtime` is reachable only through `arrears.ts`, which is a CORRECTION to a previous period — so a timesheet that HAD overtime lines would have nowhere to put them. The record's own observation (*an enum value nothing in the application produces*) measured from the other side, and the timesheet builder cannot produce one either, because overtime is a rule about a WEEK and no row in either schema holds one. (4) `employeeId: number` against a uuid. **The loop is therefore not closable at this joint**, and the reason is a modelling one rather than a bug: `example` prices a CONTRACT and a workforce product establishes a MEASUREMENT, and the only bridge available re-derives the contract from the measurement and then pays the contract. Whether the fix is a third basis (`measured`, whose lines ARE the gross), or a `Payslip` that can be drafted from lines rather than from a window, is the open question. Nothing here is a defect in what `example` ships — it is the input shape being the one thing that was taken on faith · [employment.ts § annualGross](example/api/src/domain/payroll/employment.ts) · [payslip.ts § draftPayslip](example/api/src/domain/payroll/payslip.ts) · [handoff.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/src/domain/payroll/handoff.ts) · [hours.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/test/hours.test.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-1211"></a>FJS-1211 | repo · litestone | **Five of `PHILOSOPHY.md` §V's nine questions have a generated artefact to answer them from, and the two about VOCABULARY are not among them — so *is this a new concept* is answered from memory on every proposal that asks it.** | open | 2026-09-20 | Measured over the 28 committed snapshots the `snapshots` CI phase gates. **Five questions have one and it is direct**: *derived* has the derivations themselves (`ddl`, `jsonschema`, `access`, `release`, `routes`, `principal`, `jobs`, `notifications`), *owner* has [seams.snapshot.md](seams.snapshot.md), *boundary* has [exports.snapshot.md](exports.snapshot.md) plus `surface` and `principal`, *failure* has [errors.snapshot.md](packages/junction/errors.snapshot.md) and `access`, *silence* has [invariants.snapshot.md](invariants.snapshot.md). **Two are partial and they are the front half.** *Origin* has nothing that lists where each truth lives — `seams` lists handoffs, which is not the same claim. *Concept* has [catalog.snapshot.md](packages/litestone/catalog.snapshot.md), every word a `.lite` file can hold with its completeness asserted against the parser — and **no other realm has an equivalent**; there is no catalog command outside litestone, so Mesa's blocks, Sierra's targets and the UI kit's terms are in nobody's index. *Complexity* has none and never will. **What is owed is one place holding every term the framework defines — an FJS dictionary — so the mental model can be READ rather than recalled.** The reason to want it is the audit: [`ARCHITECT.md`](ARCHITECT.md) §2 is 22 Use/Not rows, 12 clarifications and 5 terms under *Not yet named*, every one of them a hand-written claim, and **nothing grades whether the code still uses the left column** — a word three packages enforce and a word the docs alone use read identically from §2, which is [FJS-D190](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d190)'s argument about invariants arriving one realm over. **The design turns on one question and it should be ruled before anything is written: is the dictionary DERIVED or AUTHORED?** §2 is authored, so generating a second list beside it fails *another origin of truth* by construction; the honest shapes are either that §2 becomes generated and the authored claim moves down to the places that enforce it, or that the dictionary derives only what has an enforcer and cites §2 for the rest, marking a term with no enforcer the way `invariants.snapshot.md` marks a `none` row. Three sources can already be read: litestone's catalog, `bridge-index` through `seams`, and `DECISIONS.md`, where most of §2's clarifications already cite the `FJS-D##` that coined or refused the noun. **The name `lexicon` is taken** — [`IDEAS/lexicon.md`](IDEAS/lexicon.md) is the i18n half `FJS-D12` did not reach, a different thing entirely. · [PHILOSOPHY.md](PHILOSOPHY.md) §V · [decision-rules](.claude/skills/decision-rules/SKILL.md) § What each one catches · blocked by `FJS-D1050` |

Re-verified and repaired 2026-08-06; `bun run bench` now exists. What is still missing is a **gate**: CI exists and has no bench phase ([FJS-009](#fjs-009)), there are no committed baseline numbers, and absolute µs are not comparable across machines — the only method that showed anything was interleaving the same bench against the pre-change tree on one box. `packages/mesa/bench/` (`bun run bench`) gates DOM mutations and bytes against a committed baseline and is run by hand; nothing calls it. `IDEAS/performance-regression-watch.md` is the design for the gate. **The 2026-10-09 performance audit re-ran all three benches and puts its open tail here** (one machine's numbers): P3 splitStatements allocates per character, 14 ms per 157 KB of DDL and 27% of a fresh boot, ~1 ms with char-code dispatch; P4 the predicate tokenizer (now toolbelt/src/predicate/tokenize.js) is 9.5 ms of a 22 ms parse, and a sticky-regex lexer produced the same 20,978 tokens in 1.84 ms — orion shares it and error positions must not move; P5–P7 take a tenant reopen from ~20 to ~8 ms: lazy root and asSystem() tables, a one-pass buildCoFkMap (O(models² × relations) today), and the WeakMap over schema maps that H7 promised and never applied; P9–P10 take an autoMigrate miss from ~90 to ~45 ms: introspect's ~7 uncached prepares per table, and a pristine schema rebuilt per tenant of one parse; R9 @from(count) over an unindexed foreign key is 7.1 ms per 100 rows against 56 µs indexed, which advise should flag, and @sequence still runs one counter statement per row in createMany; B9 the device worker is FIFO, so a whole-list write-through sits in front of the first offline read — coalesce write-throughs per model per tick in Sierra. Opportunistic, each sub-µs to a few ms: R10 policy SQL recompiled per query, R12 per-call allocations, P8 a new $schema per client so junction's JSON-schema cache misses per tenant, P11 validate()'s find-by-name inside per-field loops, P12 DDL regenerated per tenant create and per boot hash, B6 clearBindings with no params, B7 the JSONL cold load (uncapped heap, no early stop at limit), B8 the LRU re-link per hit, S5 Studio inlining each row's JSON twice, S10 /api/refs as 17 synchronous git calls. **The method gap is unchanged**, and the audit found one more piece of it: the trail's counter and @sequence statements bypass $tapQuery, so statement counts under-report by design, and a tap on the raw handle would make the bench honest | open | 2026-10-09 | [litestone bench/PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md](packages/litestone/bench/PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md) § Re-verified |

| <a id="fjs-2287"></a>FJS-2287 | caravan | **unique holds while a job runs, so a one-per-key worker cannot queue its own successor: work that must run until its key is drained is one long-lived handler, and the moment between its last read and its end needs a cron watcher to catch the dispatch the lock refused** | open | 2026-10-10 | Measured 2026-10-10, serpgrid stressor Q6: one DataForSEO collector per agency (the vendor's limit is per account), dispatched under unique: scan-collect:<agencyId>. | <a id="fjs-2282"></a>FJS-2282 | mesa | **On the terminal target a button whose only content is an `aria-hidden` icon paints as `[  ]`: its `aria-label` is never read, so every icon-only control in the kit is a blank button** | open | 2026-10-09 | Found 2026-10-09 by the mesa-IR dialog slice. A browser's name for that button is its label, and a screen reader speaks it; a terminal paints only visible text. | <a id="fjs-1567"></a>FJS-1567 | portal | **Portal, the search stressor: page capture does not follow a <meta http-equiv=refresh> redirect, and a capture that reads 0 words is still status ok, so a redirect stub or a client-rendered page is kept as an empty copy with nothing to say so** | open | 2026-09-29 | Found seeding the knight persona (2026-09-29). https://www.conventionalcommits.org/ answers 200 with a 208-byte page whose only content is a meta refresh to /en/; https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/ answers 200 with 152 bytes refreshing to /essay/local-first. [fetch.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/fetch.ts) follows HTTP redirects only (redirect: 'manual', each hop re-checked by the SSRF guard), and nothing in api/src/domain/pages reads a refresh. Both were kept as status ok, words 0, finalUrl the stub. A client-rendered page does the same: https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/ (content in a <template>, filled by script) is ok with 0 words; not a parser defect, but indistinguishable from one on the page. [capture.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/capture.ts) writes status ok for any parse, and capture.ts:71 (hasCopy = words != null) then treats the empty copy as kept, so a link check never retries it. Fix: follow a same-document meta refresh (delay 0, http(s) only) as one more guarded hop; and write a 0-word parse as failed (for example 'the page had no readable text'), keeping link live, so the page shows the capture failed and offers Capture again. Seen with FJS-1566, whose empty copies are the same symptom from a different cause |
| <a id="fjs-1564"></a>FJS-1564 | repo · cli · css · sierra · vscode | **No surface or realm has a color of its own, so nothing a developer sees says at a glance which part of the app it came from** | open | 2026-09-29 | The goal: pick one primary color per realm (Data, API, UI, plus Deployment and Testing) and per surface (api, web, site, widgets, extension, desktop, cli), and carry it everywhere a dev sees that part of the app until the color alone says where they are. Today the nearest thing is accidental: `fli dev` prefixes come from bun run --parallel ([new.md:265](packages/cli/commands/project/new.md#L265)), which colors by script ORDER, so dev:web is yellow in one app and cyan in the next. **Where it would help:** (1) fli dev log prefixes and its banner (slot · web 8003 · API 8103), each surface and port in its color; (2) every realm-tagged log line -- litestone, caravan, junction $.log -- so a scrolling terminal sorts itself; (3) fli ci phases, fli proves / prove, fli check findings, fli next and fli ws:atlas, tagged by realm or surface; (4) fli new and fli make:* output naming what they created; (5) a FrameworkError's terminal print naming the realm it was thrown in; (6) the browser tab in dev -- a tinted favicon per surface so web and site tabs differ, the Sierra error overlay border, the dev banner; (7) Litestone Studio chrome in the Data color, Junction devtools in API, each registerDevService entry in its own; (8) the VS Code extension -- file icons for .lite (Data) and .mesa (UI), folder colors for api/ web/ site/ db/, the status bar; (9) docs -- ARCHITECT.md's realm diagram, README § Project Structure, VOCABULARY entries, the docs site, the data-/api-/ui-hazards skill headers, audit artifacts; (10) Basecamp and Outpost -- an app's surfaces in their colors across servers, deploys and releases; (11) test output -- the Suite realm, and which drive (API tier or browser) a failure came from; (12) the ISSUES.md Pkg column as fli next and register views render it. **Constraints:** one owner for the table (surface → realm, hue, ANSI and hex), most likely toolbelt since cli, css, sierra and the vscode extension all read it -- or beside CAT in [ports.js](packages/cli/core/ports.js), already one row per surface -- never a copy per package (Invariant 4); in @frontierjs/css it is a tone for DEV chrome only and never reaches a shipped app's styling (Invariant 13); color is never the only signal -- a label or glyph goes with it, NO_COLOR and 16-color terminals degrade cleanly, and the palette is checked for color-blind separation; "surface" already means a background layer in @frontierjs/css (surface.css), so the naming must not add a third sense. **Open questions (decision-rules):** realm as hue family and surface as a shade inside it (web, site, widgets, extension and desktop are all UI) or a distinct hue per surface; what color cli gets; whether Deployment and Testing get colors or stay neutral |

| <a id="fjs-1268"></a>FJS-1268 | cli · notifications | **`fli check`'s `surface-src` grades FILES at a surface root and never directories, so a whole directory of application source sitting beside `src/` is unreported — and it is the location `@frontierjs/notifications` probes FIRST.** | open | 2026-09-22 | Found wiring reminders on connectteam Phase 6. Invariant 3 is *a surface keeps its source in `src/`, and only its entry beside it*, and the rule enforces it: a stray `api/probe.ts` written during this session was reported on the next run, by name, with the reason. `resolveNotificationsDir` probes `[resolve(base, 'notifications'), resolve(base, 'src', 'notifications')]` and takes the first that exists ([loader.ts:56](packages/notifications/loader.ts)), where `base` is the directory of the entry — so for an app whose entry is `api/index.ts` the preferred location is `api/notifications/`, a directory of app source beside `api/src/`. **Measured:** `api/notifications/ShiftReminder.notification.ts` in place, `fli check --only surface-src` → *nothing to report*. The same file one directory further in is where `example/` puts it and is what this app declares. Two small things, either of which closes it: have the rule walk directories at a surface root as well as files, and/or reverse the package's probe order so the layout it prefers is the one the invariant wants. The probe order matters on its own — an app that lets itself be probed rather than declaring `notifications:` gets whichever it happens to have created. · [loader.ts](packages/notifications/loader.ts) · Invariant 3 |

| <a id="fjs-1256"></a>FJS-1256 | junction | **A custom method has ONE answer, and it is both the caller's result and the payload broadcast to every other tab — so a write whose useful answer is a report makes every connected client log *ignored an update with no id* and drop it.** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Driven in a browser**, connectteam Phase 5. `timesheets.build` writes a `Timesheet` and one `TimesheetLine` per measured clock entry, and what the caller needs back is the report — how many lines, which clocks were still running, which days had no pay rate — so it answers `{ sheet, lines, stillRunning, noRate }`. That answer is announced on the service's channel under the method's own name, and junction's client logged `[Junction] ignored an update with no id — it cannot be matched to a row. An announcement carries the record it is about.` The documented instrument is `$.dispatch = false`, which is a boolean: the app can announce a shape no client can use, or announce nothing and leave every other tab unaware that a timesheet now exists. There is no third spelling — `$.dispatch` cannot name the row to announce, and returning the row instead loses the report the caller came for. The row's own guidance names the read-shaped case (*a count, a report, a credential* → `$.dispatch = false`); this is the write-shaped one, where silence has a cost. A `$.announce(row)` beside `$.dispatch`, or a method-level `announces:` naming which part of the answer is the record, would close it · [timesheets.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/src/services/timesheets.service.ts) · Seen again 2026-10-09 in the serpgrid stressor, Phase 4: clients.provision answers an outcome ({ outcome, clientId, locationId }), and driven in Chrome every open tab was refused it as a Client ('every one of 2 subscribers was refused a clients broadcast') until the method said $.dispatch = false by hand · [serpgrid clients.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/serpgrid/api/src/services/clients.service.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-1262"></a>FJS-1262 | junction | **A custom method whose payload is legitimately empty cannot be called over HTTP: `{}` is read as *no body* and answered 400, while the same call over the WebSocket works — so the transport the browser prefers hides it.** | open | 2026-10-12 | **Measured**, connectteam Phase 5. `POST /api/clockEntries` with `X-Service-Method: stop` and body `{}` → `400 {"name":"BadRequest","message":"Request body is required"}`; the same request with `{"shiftId":null}` → `200` and the row; no body at all → the same 400. The browser never sees it, because the client prefers the socket once connected and the WS path carries `{}` happily — driven: the *Clock out* button on the employee screen works in a tab and the identical call from `curl` does not. Every non-browser caller is on the HTTP path: a script, a webhook, a native shell, a server-to-server call, and `fli`-driven smoke tests. *Clock me out*, *revoke my other sessions*, *mark all read* are ordinary methods whose payload is nothing, and the workaround is to invent a key · [body.ts](packages/junction/src/transport/body.ts) · [clock-entries.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/src/services/clock-entries.service.ts) · Seen again 2026-10-12 in ELA's Phase Q5: surveyTemplates.preview called over HTTP with {} answers 'Request body is required' · fjs-prototypes/ela PLAN.md § Phase Q |
| <a id="fjs-1234"></a>FJS-1234 | litestone · caravan | **A predicate that depends on a ZONE held in a column cannot be a `where`, so deferred work over per-row wall-clock times is a full scan of the window: every candidate row is read and all but a few are discarded in application code.** | open | 2026-09-21 | Found building reminders on the calendly stressor (PLAN.md § Q9). The product rule is *08:00 on the morning of, in the INVITEE's zone* — the one people actually want, as against *24 hours before*, which is easy precisely because a duration needs no zone. **The query that should exist cannot be written.** `booking.inviteeTimeZone` is a column, so *has 08:00 passed for this row* is a calendar calculation per row against a different zone per row. `where` has no zone-aware operator and no index can serve one, so the sweep bounds what it can — `startsAt` between now and now+48h, an ordinary instant comparison — and asks the real question in JavaScript. **Measured on a small database: `considered 60, sent 2`.** The ratio is set by the horizon and the spread of zones, not by how many reminders are due, so it does not improve with scale — it is 2 sends from 60 reads today and 2 from 60,000 on a real calendar. **Re-measured at workforce scale on connectteam 2026-09-22, and the claim holds with one correction.** 4,000 published shifts over a fortnight, 600 people, 8 sites, a 48-hour horizon, a five-minute cron. ONE fire at 07:00Z — 08:00 where half the workforce is, the most productive instant of that day — **considered 566, sent 96**, discarding **264 pending + 206 tooLate** on the predicate that cannot be lowered and **0 past** on the one that can, in **773 ms**. Over a whole day the same window is re-read 288 times for the same 173 reminders the employer owes: **165,744 rows read, 173 sent — 1 send per 958 rows**, and **~180 seconds of CPU a day** to do it (24 fires measured at 621 ms each across the block holding both zones' 08:00; the read total is arithmetic on the measured per-fire figure, the sends are measured). **The correction is which of the two terms matters.** Moving the same 600 people from 2 zones (the brief's: Lisbon and the Azores, ONE hour apart) to 12 spread around the world left `considered` **identical at 566** and moved the sends only from 96 to 81 — spreading people over more zones spreads their 08:00s over the clock rather than changing how many there are. **So the cost is set by the horizon alone, and the spread is second order**: an employer with one hour of spread pays a global calendar's price. That removes the one escape a reader might infer from this row — that a geographically tight product is cheap. **And the cheap fix this row floats does not reach this case.** A `@generated` column holding the reminder instant fails here for a stronger reason than *cannot do arithmetic*: the zone is `User.timeZone`, which is **two relations** from `Shift` (`Shift → Employee → User`), and *which* morning is itself undecided between `Shift.onDate` (the day the manager typed, in the SITE's zone) and `startsAt` read in the person's — two columns the schema does not relate. Measured: the same shift is `tooLate` for a Lisbon employee and `pending` for an Azorean one, with reminder instants a DAY apart. **`tooLate` is a second consequence worth naming**, at 206 of 566 rows in one fire: a rule stated as a wall clock has shifts it can never remind at all — every shift starting before 08:00 local, which in a field workforce is the early turn. A rule stated as a duration has no such case, which is precisely why building that one would have measured nothing. · driven in connectteam `api/test/reminders.test.ts` § 1, § 6 **This is [FJS-1214](#fjs-1214)'s gap in a second place and the consequence is different enough to be its own row.** 1214 is about DECLARATION — a recurring wall-clock window cannot be spelled in `.lite`. This is about QUERY: the same absence of zone awareness means a zoned predicate cannot be pushed down, and the cost lands on background work rather than on a form. The arithmetic exists and is correct — `fromWall`/`partsIn` in toolbelt answered every DST case in `api/test/reminders.test.ts` first time, including a Tokyo booking whose reminder falls on the previous UTC date — so what is missing is not the maths but anywhere to put it that the database can see. **The cron half is not a defect and is worth stating so the row is not read as one.** `handle(…, { cron, timeZone })` binds ONE zone per schedule (measured: `registrations()` returns `timeZone: null` for an unzoned expression), which is right — a schedule is a statement about the app, not about a row. It is *because* that is right that the work has to become a sweep, and the sweep is where the missing predicate bites. **What would close it:** a zone-aware comparison litestone can lower — the same word [FJS-1214](#fjs-1214) asks for, reused in `where` — or, far cheaper and worth considering first, a `@generated` column holding the reminder instant, which fails today for the reason `Booking.endsAt` already documents in this app's schema: a generated column cannot reach across a relation or do arithmetic on one. **What is NOT a finding, measured and cleared:** caravan's dispatch door. `delay` is a duration and the `jobs` table stores `run_at`, an instant, which looked like `FJS-D143`'s category error one layer down — it is not. The conversion is exact (measured: `run_at` landed on the target instant, off by 0 ms), and a `runAt` option does not exist rather than being silently ignored, so TypeScript refuses it at the call site; reaching it needs a deliberate `as any`. The queue contributed durability, one-fire-per-cluster and retries, and none of Q9's difficulty came from it · [caravan/src/cron.ts](packages/caravan/src/cron.ts) · [FJS-1214](#fjs-1214) · [FJS-D143](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d143) · blocked by `FJS-D908` · blocked by `FJS-D1108` |
| <a id="fjs-1235"></a>FJS-1235 | cli | **The scaffolded `dev:api` watcher does not restart when `db/schema.lite` changes, because the schema is read from disk at runtime and is not in the module graph — so editing the schema silently does nothing and the API keeps serving the old one, answering confidently wrong.** | open | 2026-10-08 | Found on the calendly stressor; cost two stalls before the cause was understood, each spent debugging an app that was correct. **Measured, with a control, on one running process:** `PORT=8102 bun --watch run api/index.ts`, then — (1) a real content change to `api/src/core/db.ts` → the app **restarted** (a second boot banner in the log); (2) a real content change to `db/schema.lite`, including adding an actual column to a model → **no restart**, no log line, no warning. The control is the point: the watcher works, and it is not watching the file that defines the data. **Both halves are scaffolded by `fli new` and they disagree.** `api/src/core/db.ts` builds a schema PATH — `fileURLToPath(new URL('../../../db/schema.lite', import.meta.url))` — and hands it to `createClient`, so the schema is opened with `fs` at runtime and never imported. `bun --watch` watches the module graph. A path string is not an import, so the most-edited file in a schema-first framework is the one file the dev loop ignores. **The symptom is the bad kind: silence plus a plausible wrong answer.** A column added to the schema is absent from the running API, so a request writing it fails validation for a field the developer is looking straight at, and a policy edited to open a door stays shut. Nothing says *restart me*; `fli check` is green because the source is fine; and the natural conclusion is that the schema change is wrong. **Same shape as [FJS-1232](#fjs-1232)** — two scaffolded pieces that do not agree, with nothing announcing it — and this app has now hit that shape three times in two days ([FJS-1233](#fjs-1233) is the third). **Fix:** make the dev script watch the schema — `bun --watch --watch-extensions .lite` if it supports one, otherwise `bunx --bun concurrently` or a small chokidar wrapper in the scaffolded script — or, better, have litestone `createClient` register the schema path with the runtime's watcher when one is present, so every app gets it without a script change. Cheapest interim: one line in the scaffolded `AGENTS.md` under *What a generic habit gets wrong here*, since that file already exists to catch exactly this class · [FJS-1232](#fjs-1232) · [FJS-1233](#fjs-1233) · Seen again in stressor ela: a migrated @generated column was refused as an unknown orderBy until the dev API was restarted. Measured: an `import '../db/schema.lite' with { type: 'text' }` makes bun --watch restart, but api/src/core/db.ts is also imported by vite/site builds where the attribute breaks — the fix is fli's or litestone's |
| <a id="fjs-1231"></a>FJS-1231 | ui | **`<Select>` given a `value` that matches none of its options renders blank and says nothing — which is indistinguishable from *nothing is chosen*, and is how a wrong handler presents itself.** | open | 2026-09-21 | Reported on the calendly stressor as *selecting a day makes the selection disappear*. **The cause was the app's**, and this row is not a complaint about the contract: `<Select>` and `<Input>` wire `on:change={onchange}` / `oninput?.(e)` straight to the DOM and their headers say *Native event callbacks*, so a handler written as `(v) => Number(v)` receives an Event, `Number(Event)` is `NaN`, and the control then holds a value no `<option>` has. The browser renders that as an empty box. **What is missing is the sentence.** The component knows, at render time, that it was handed a non-null `value` matching none of its normalized options — it has already built `flatOptions` — and it renders blank instead of saying so. Nothing else catches it either: the page compiles, `fli check` is green, and there is no console output, so the only signal is a control that silently discards what you pick. **The kit already holds this exact principle** and applies it one case over. `optionsNote` exists because *an empty list and a list nobody could fetch render identically, and a person [cannot tell]* ([utils.js:260](packages/ui/utils.js)), and `truncationNote` exists for the same reason. A value that matches no option is the third member of that family and the only one with no note. A `console.warn` naming the component, the value and the option count would have turned a blank box into a one-line answer; a visible note is probably wrong here, since the state is usually a bug rather than something to tell an end user about. Worth pairing with [FJS-1230](#fjs-1230), which recommends the same remedy for a different silent discard, and with [FJS-1208](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1208). Three components in one kit now drop what they were given without a word, which is a house style rather than three bugs · [Select.mesa](packages/ui/components/forms/Select.mesa) · [utils.js:260](packages/ui/utils.js) · [FJS-1230](#fjs-1230) |

Low because a host can operate orion without them: the flows and runs screens cover authoring and watching, and metrics is the only one an operator asks for by name. Filed so the mockup's remaining lines are accounted for rather than implied · [pages.jsx](packages/orion/mockup/ui/components/pages.jsx) · [web/routes](packages/orion/web/routes) |

| <a id="fjs-1158"></a>FJS-1158 | junction | **The announcement check warns that a write answered a projection when the only missing column is one the caller can never read**: `flowCredentials.create() answered 9 of 7 columns — missing secret`, on every create of a model with an `@encrypted` column below system. | open | 2026-10-09 | `announcementPayload` compares the answered keys against every column `modelColumns` lists, protected ones included, and a non-system client strips `@encrypted`, `@guarded` and `@secret` from every row it reads. So the warning fires on a derived CRUD service that answered the whole row it could, re-reads the row by id (which strips the same column again), and tells the author to answer a column they are not allowed to see. | <a id="fjs-747"></a>FJS-747 | junction | **The suite exits 1 with `0 fail` and no test named, roughly once in ten runs.** Seen three times across 2026-09-02/03, always the same shape: `bun run test` reports `1893 pass · 0 fail`, prints no `(fail)` line anywhere, and exits non-zero — so CI would go red naming nothing. **Two things this row used to say are measured wrong** (2026-09-05, bun 1.3.11). *The stated hypothesis*: an unhandled rejection escaping a test cannot be it — bun installs its own `unhandledRejection` listener, so `process.listenerCount('unhandledRejection')` is **1** inside `bun test`, junction's `listenerCount === 0` guard therefore never installs its rejection handler here at all, and an escaped rejection is attributed by bun to whatever test is running as a `(fail)`, which is the opposite of the observed shape. *The proposed instrument*: a preload registering `process.on('unhandledRejection')` **never fires** — confirmed with the preload loading (it printed) and the rejection still going to bun's own reporter. The remaining window is a throw landing BETWEEN files, where no test is in scope to attribute it to. `process.exitCode = 1` reproduces the reported shape EXACTLY (`1 pass · 0 fail`, no `(fail)` line, exit 1) and nothing in `src/` or `test/` writes it, so it is a shape match rather than the cause — a dependency doing it would look the same. **12 consecutive clean runs** on 2026-09-05, so it is still not reproducible on demand | open | 2026-09-05 | [test/](packages/junction/test) · [app.ts `crashStop`](packages/junction/src/core/app.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-610"></a>FJS-610 | example | **A soft decline is never re-presented, so every invoice is charged exactly once and the distinction the code makes between soft and hard buys nothing.** `declineKind` separates *the money may be there tomorrow* from *this card will never work*, and the whole value of the first is that the clock keeps running and the charge is tried again. Nothing tries it again: `subscription-renew` dispatches `invoice-collect` once, and dunning moves STATES — `Invoice`'s two `@@commitment`s lapse at the grace and cancel at the deadline, `recoverIfClear` recovers when the ledger is clean — and dispatches nothing. So a soft-declined invoice sits `issued` until the deadline cancels the subscription, having been presented one time. **Caravan's retry ladder does not cover it and cannot**: a transport failure throws and retries, but a decline is a domain ANSWER returned as a value, which exits the ladder successfully. The fix is a re-presentment with a clock of its own, under `unique` for [`FJS-609`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-609)'s reason, with the cadence a decision rather than a default — a shop that re-presents daily for 21 days is a shop the card networks notice. Not a defect in anything built: every piece is correct on its own, and this is the half the design implies and nobody wrote. `verify:collect` asserts the soft decline leaves the subscription alone, which is true and is not the same as the money being asked for again | open | 2026-08-30 | [schema.lite `Invoice`](example/db/schema.lite) · [billing.ts `declineKind`](example/api/src/domain/billing/billing.ts) · blocked by `FJS-D907` |

## Needs a decision

These are questions, not defects. A ruling moves to `DECISIONS.md` and closes the
row here. **This table is the questions with an id; most open questions are argued
inside an IDEAS paper's `## Open questions` and stay there.** `fli decisions` reads
both as one queue, and a question becomes pickable — by `fli decide` or on `fli gui`
— once its bullet carries lettered options and a `**Recommend X**` line. A row's
cell cannot hold options, so they go in the paper its Detail links.

| <a id="fjs-d1131"></a>FJS-D1131 | litestone · junction | **Is a foreign wire format (Bitwarden's Type: 2, RevisionDate, Object: "cipher" — names and values fixed by a client somebody else wrote) the plugin's alone, or may the schema point at it — @map renames the column and nothing a caller touches, @label is a human title, an enum member carries no value** | vaultwarden Q1's pre-run guess is 'a ruling, not a word' · [open-questions.md § Cannot say C8](../fjs-prototypes/vaultwarden/discovery/open-questions.md) · Measured, vaultwarden Phase 1 (bw 2026.10.0 logging in with TOTP against the real app, measure/bw-login.mjs green). The client asked for exactly nine things to log in, sync and list: POST /identity/accounts/prelogin/password, POST /identity/connect/token (form-urlencoded; grant_type password with twoFactorToken/Provider/Remember in the SAME request when a code is given, and refresh_token), GET /api/config, GET /api/sync, GET /api/accounts/revision-date, POST /api/accounts/key-management/user-key-id, plus the legacy prelogin paths. All nine are raw routes in one app plugin (api/src/bitwarden/plugin.ts); no service was touched and the model names never reach the wire. Four things the framework had to be worked around on: (1) the access token must be a JWT the client decodes (sub, email, sstamp, exp), and Junction resolves every Bearer through auth.verifySession, so an Object.create(auth) wrapper unwraps a sid claim — six lines, verifySession IS the seam, cleared; (2) the OAuth error JSON (invalid_grant + error_description, 400) is translated by the plugin in a try/catch around auth.login, a second thrown-value→HTTP translator beside toResponse (Invariant 4) with no per-route hook to hand the owner a dialect; (3) /identity/* sits outside apiPrefix and so on app.http.router, which drops the request scope (FJS-3104); (4) Junction serves no TLS and the client refuses http (FJS-3105). The pre-run guess holds as far as it goes — an app plugin over raw routes — and the ruling should say what the framework owes it: the request scope on every route it registers, and a way for a plugin to own the error translation for ITS routes; the schema points at nothing (Type: 2, RevisionDate stay the plugin's). |

## Closed

Kept so a stale document cannot reopen them. Newest first.

**Older closures live in [ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md).** This
section holds the recent ones and is trimmed past ~40 rows by `fli register:archive`;
the archive holds the rest, verbatim. An id is never reused, so a `FJS-###` named anywhere in the repo
resolves in one file or the other.

| Id | Title | Closed | How |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <a id="fjs-3174"></a>FJS-3174 | basecamp — **Orion's webhooks are answered with the SPA, because the proxy path list drops a raw route with a template anywhere in it** | 2026-10-17 | Only a path STARTING templated (the CRUD handler) is skipped; a template further in proxies by its first segment, so `/orion` is on the list (57 to 58). The services.test.ts skip got the same change and goes red naming `/orion` under the old rule; verify:caddy 12/12 · [api-paths.js](packages/basecamp/web/config/api-paths.js) · [services.test.ts](packages/basecamp/api/test/services.test.ts) |

| <a id="fjs-d668"></a>FJS-D668 | ui — **Should a named slot block (slot="header") satisfy a component's snippet prop of the same name — once in Mesa, or per component, or not at all?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D668`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d668): **D** — the compiler owns it, and snippets are the one runtime system: `<h2 slot="header">…</h2>` lowers to `{#snippet header()}<h2>…</h2>{/snippet}`, and a component's `<slot name="header">fallback</slot>` lowers to `{@render header?.()}` with the fallback. `attachNamedSlotLegacy`, `makeSlots` and the slot runtime are deleted, along with Form's hand fallback; `slot=` carrying arguments is refused, naming the snippet form; a name that is neither slot nor prop keeps `FJS-926`'s warning. | <a id="fjs-3094"></a>FJS-3094 | litestone — **FileStorage has no streaming entry: readValue reads a File through arrayBuffer(), fromPath is readFileSync and provider.put takes the whole object, so an upload costs 3.6x its size in heap and an app that streams must write the ref itself** | 2026-10-16 | readValue read every File and Blob whole through arrayBuffer() and fromPath through readFileSync, then handed the bytes to provider.put. Now a File, Blob or fromPath (opened with openAsBlob) reaches put as the Blob itself, and only its first 4096 bytes are read, for sniff. LocalProvider pipes a Blob to disk. A fromPath of 200 MB peaked at +199 MB RSS (VmHWM) at HEAD and +26–31 MB after. An app that streams an upload to disk can now hand create() fromPath(tmp) or Bun.file(tmp), and serialize writes the ref, so the app no longer builds the ref itself. test/file-from-path.test.ts § FJS-3094: a Blob whose arrayBuffer/bytes/text throw is stored and sniffed, and fromPath reaches put as a Blob. Still open: S3 hashes the payload for its signature, so it reads a Blob whole (FJS-3115), and the transport's own copies are junction's (FJS-3093). A caller's JSON ref string is accepted as stored (FJS-3114). |

| <a id="fjs-d1116"></a>FJS-D1116 | auth — **Which people may auth's people service reach — by what rule does it decide a person is inside the operator's tenant?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D1116`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1116): **A** — derive it from the app's own resolver: `aim()` re-resolves the PERSON with `app.runAs(person, { tenant: app.tenant() }, () => app.withDb((_, user) => user))`, so the app's principal resolver answers in the operator's tenant. The person is reached only where the tenancy claim it returns equals `app.tenant()`, otherwise 404 as today. `standingLevel` grades that re-resolved principal. `remove`, which deletes the whole `User`, is refused below SYSADMIN when the person holds a membership outside this tenant. One rule for both shapes: an `accountId` tenancy and a membership tenancy each answer through their own claim. No tenancy declared means no scoping, which is today's null-`accountId` operator. Uses existing seams only and adds no option. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |

| <a id="fjs-620"></a>FJS-620 | litestone — **Findings from the performance audit that are in no other register, so they depend on somebody reading a July document.** [`FJS-112`](#fjs-112) exists and is about the METHOD — no owner, no gate, no committed baselines — and the still-open list it names in passing covers H8, H9, JSONL cold-load streaming, S3 streaming/multipart and a low-impact tail. Five medium findings are named in neither it nor either idea document: **M4** nested writes — the atomicity half is closed by [`FJS-638`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-638), which put nested writes inside the transaction machinery, and what stands is that they run one statement per child; **M5** variable-length `IN (?,?,…)` lists compile a distinct statement per value-count and churn the 500-entry LRU, **and there is no chunking guard for SQLite's bind-variable limit**, which is a correctness cliff rather than a slow one; **M11** (closed: `resolveAllRowCounts` counts each table once through `countRows`, `getTableStats` keeps the whole-file pricing for the one-table bytes limit; `test/transform-row-counts.test.ts`); **M12** the retention pass, whose first-line early exit and O(n²) `shift()` loop both landed but whose un-indexed `DELETE … WHERE createdAt < ?` still full-scans unless the app happened to index the column — the audit's fix was to auto-create it when a `database` block declares `retention`. **M7 was the fifth and is closed** ([`FJS-619`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-619)). Not one issue per finding, because the audit is the detail and duplicating it here is how the two disagree; this is the pointer that makes them open. **The 2026-10-09 performance audit re-confirmed M4 and M5, measured M5's cliff, and adds M6 here**: M5 (its R6) — 64 IN-list lengths compile 64 statements, the LRU churn that triggered [FJS-2309](#fjs-2309)'s finalize; 40,000 values work (13.7 ms), 100,000 throw Bun's raw *expected 34464 values*, and the wasm engine's default limit is 32,766. **M5 closed 2026-10-10**: past four values a list binds as one JSON array through `inList` (query.js) — the caller's `in`/`notIn`/bare array/`hasNone`, every include and `_count` key list, the soft-delete cascade and restore, the edge lookups, FTS rowids, and a policy's list against a column. The audit's `SELECT value` was wrong on a TEXT column: a json_each value takes no affinity, so `name IN (1)` missed the text '1' a bound list matches; `CAST(value AS TEXT)` lets the column's own affinity convert it back, exact on TEXT, INTEGER and REAL, float precision included. It is wrong on a column with no affinity, so the trail's `Any` columns and expression operands (a json_each value, a json_extract path) take the value uncast, and a @from operand, a policy path, a caller with no field kinds and a value JSON cannot carry keep the bound list, as do composite keys. Proved by test/in-list.test.ts (a hand-written bound list as the oracle, column type by column type, both directions; 60 lengths are one statement; 100,000 values answer) and a browser-drive case (numbers asked of a String column, 40,000 values past the wasm limit). Per execution the two forms are even up to ~20 values and JSON is ~20% slower at 100–1,000 on an already-prepared statement. sierra test:safety 12/12; basecamp verify:screens 117/118 on the 7120 slot, and its one failure (*deleting the app never landed on its environment*) fails the same with the JSON path switched off, so it is not this. M6 (R7) — the read path clones a row 3–5 times (scalars, @from, computed, field policy with delete, mirror drop) and include.js carries a second copy of the chain: 0.17 µs/row plain against 0.40 with Json + Boolean + @computed + @omit; one owned clone at the top, the include copy changed in the same commit (FJS-223). M4 (R11) — each nested child is still one full verb, and before FJS-2313 each one also paid an exists() per foreign key | 2026-10-16 | What stood under the pointer is now closed or has a row of its own. M11: getTableStats summed every table's COUNT(*) to price one row, and resolveAllRowCounts called it once per table, so a percent or size limit over T tables ran T + T² counts (156 for 12, measured). It and resolveRowCount now take a plain countRows, and only a bytes limit on one table prices a row (transform/framework.js). test/transform-row-counts.test.ts goes red at HEAD and green here. M5 was closed 2026-10-10. M12's remaining half is FJS-2291, blocked by FJS-D849; advise's retention-without-an-index already covers a model that is not soft-deleted. M6 (R7, row cloning) is FJS-3001 and M4 (R11, one statement per nested child) is FJS-3002. litestone test 7508/0 and statements ratchet green; sierra test:safety and the studio drives pass; the example drives could not start because port 8110 already answered; basecamp verify asks for --reset on a dev db holding 5 users, and transform/ is in neither app's path · [PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md](packages/litestone/bench/PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md) · [FJS-112](#fjs-112) |

| <a id="fjs-1645"></a>FJS-1645 | litestone — **loadRows holds every record of its source in memory before writing, so a 200,000-row CSV of 12.6 MB peaks at 1.4 GB RSS: about 110 times the file** | 2026-10-16 | loadRows read the whole CSV into records, kept a parallel line array, then a second array of coerced rows before the first write (200,000 rows / 20 MB: 2193 MB peak RSS). | <a id="fjs-d1089"></a>FJS-D1089 | conduit — **How does a row name a self-hosted counterparty — its address and its token, sometimes on a private network — without a stored credential going where a stranger says?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D1089`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1089): **A** — two halves, neither a new option. *The token is the row's own*: `address_from: 'request'` admits `bearer`, `api_key` and `signed` when `auth.per_caller: true`, and such a send states `grant`, refused by name (`invalid_request`, nothing sent) without it — the credential and the address are read off the same row, so the writer of the address holds the token, and `withCache` keyed on the grant keeps two rows in one tenant from sharing one cached token (`FJS-2232` per row). The register refusal stays for a process credential. *A private address is never a row's*: the public grade stays before every attempt, so a self-hosted instance behind a public name (the common case) is reached and one on a LAN or a tailnet is the operator's to declare as a fixed-address target per install, or waits for Outpost vantage, as `FJS-D1018` ruled. `allowPrivate` stays a test receiver's switch. Cost: a per-row LAN instance has no spelling until vantage; a `getFor` that ignores `grant` answers a tenant's token for every row's address, which conduit cannot see and the hazard names. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) · [conduit.ts](packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts) · [http.ts](packages/conduit/src/transports/http.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-d1080"></a>FJS-D1080 | junction — **Does createApp take one root (or import.meta.url) from which services/, jobs/, notifications/ and ../config derive, replacing autoload, caravan.jobsDir, notificationsPlugin({ notifications }) and configPath?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D1080`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1080): **A** — `createApp({ root: import.meta.url })`; `services/`, `jobs/`, `notifications/`, `../config` derive from it; a battery reads `app.root`. · [IDEAS/lockdown.md](IDEAS/lockdown.md) |
| <a id="fjs-d1079"></a>FJS-D1079 | junction — **Which one verb defines a service, and what does it return — a definition the registry builds (createService(def) → the file exports it, no factory-name rule) or a built Service?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D1079`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1079): **A** — `createService(def)` returns a definition; the file `export default`s it; the registry builds. `createBaseService` and the factory-name rule go. · [IDEAS/lockdown.md](IDEAS/lockdown.md) |
| <a id="fjs-d1077"></a>FJS-D1077 | junction · repo — **What is the one factory grammar — createX(opts) for a thing you hold, defineX(spec) for a declaration the framework reads, and a Plugin as a bare noun x(opts), with the dependency in opts rather than positional?** | 2026-10-16 | Ruled [`FJS-D1077`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1077): **A** — `createX(opts)` builds a thing you hold; `defineX(spec)` states a declaration the framework reads, one object argument, the name from the file or `spec.name`; a Plugin is a bare noun `x(opts)` because `app.configure(…)` already says *plugin*; a dependency goes in opts (`auth({ auth })`, `mail({ mailer })`), never positional. Renames: `manifestPlugin→manifest`, `metricsPlugin→metrics`, `exportPlugin→exporter`, `healthPlugin→health`, `notificationsPlugin→notifications`, `mcpPlugin→mcp`, `printerPlugin→printer`, `createAuthPlugin→auth`, `mailerPlugin→mail`, `createCaravan→caravan`, `backfills→backfill`. · [IDEAS/lockdown.md](IDEAS/lockdown.md) |

| <a id="fjs-555"></a>FJS-555 | cli · basecamp — **`example/site` and `example/widgets` build from a context holding a real `.env` with no `.dockerignore` at all.** Retitled 2026-09-13 — basecamp's half is fixed and what follows is how the class was found. Filed as: a `.dockerignore` pattern without `**` protects the context ROOT and nothing under it, so basecamp shipped a stray SQLite database into its image. Docker matches an ignore pattern with Go's `filepath.Match`, where a plain `*` does not cross a separator — measured: with `.env.*`, a root `.env.production` is excluded and `api/.env.production` is **copied**; `**/.env.*` reaches both. basecamp's file said `db/*.db`, which excluded `db/basecamp.db` and admitted `db/db/basecamp.db` — and `db/db/` is precisely what a relative `database { path }` resolved against the wrong working directory creates ([FJS-449](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-449)), git-ignored, so it appears in no diff. The Dockerfile does `COPY db ./db` and then `COPY --from=build /app /app`, so it reached the final image; `fli deploy:local` on a developer's machine therefore built an image carrying that machine's database, which is the exact hazard the file's own comment says it is guarding against. **The pattern is fixed and the class is now checked** — `fli deploy`'s `02b-build-check` step grades this over the server's real build context and refuses. **That claim was half true and is corrected 2026-08-29**: the check's classifier (`isStateFile`) graded `.db-wal` and `.db-shm` as state, and its finder (`CONTEXT_FIND`) looked for `*.db` and not the sidecars — two lists for one fact, written twice, disagreeing, with the finder's own comment claiming it was *the same list spelled for `find`*. So SQLite's sidecars were invisible to the rule that exists to catch them, and the SCAFFOLD's own `.dockerignore` still said `db/*.db`. The consequence was measured on a real deploy: the container writes `db/app.db-wal` into the mounted volume, which is inside the build context, so **every deploy after the first copied the running app's write-ahead log into the image** — one deployment's live data in the artefact, and a moving image digest, which under `04c-journal` made an unchanged redeploy mint a new Release. The finder is now built from the classifier's list and a test asserts they agree; the scaffold writes the `**/` forms basecamp already had. What is left is the other apps: `example/site` and `example/widgets` build from an `example/` context holding a real `.env`, with no `.dockerignore` at all, and both are reported as a warning because their runtime stages copy subtrees rather than the whole — the value stops in an intermediate layer on the build host, readable with `docker build --target build`, rather than shipping | 2026-10-15 | Added example/.dockerignore (**/.env, **/.env.*, !**/.env.example, **/dist, node_modules, job queue, audit trail, db write-ahead sidecars) at the context root both site/deploy and widgets/deploy build from, so the real .env no longer reaches the build stage; the site's data stays in the context because its prerender load() reads it at build time. Proved by packages/cli/test/build-check.test.js 'example/.dockerignore' (red with the file emptied, green with it), which grades the real file and both real Dockerfiles through inspectBuild. · [build-check.js](packages/cli/core/build-check.js) · [.dockerignore](packages/basecamp/.dockerignore) |

| <a id="fjs-1028"></a>FJS-1028 | cli — **`test/server.test.js` asserts that a well-known DEV port is unbound, so five rows go red whenever anybody is developing.** `a tool moves down → up → down as something binds its port` takes `rows.find(r => r.kind === 'tool')` and opens with `expect(await at()).toBe('down')`; the four `GET /api/health/:id` rows below it start a server on that same port. Is port 8503 in use?`. **The suite is green only when nobody is working.** It is the repo's own formula read backwards — env 7 is test, env 8 is dev, and a test asserting about ports belongs on the 7 tier — but the tools block is DEFINED as dev/tooling/project-0 and reserved whole, so the rows genuinely carry 8500-series numbers and the fix is not a digit swap. **What earns it a row rather than a note is the direction it fails in**: loudly, locally, and looking exactly like a real regression. Measured three times in one session — twice inside a CI verdict that was otherwise green, once while grading an unrelated change to `02-publish-all` — and each time it cost a fresh investigation to rule out. `FLI_PORT` is already overridden to `13141` at the top of this same file, so the precedent for isolating a port here exists and was not extended to the rows that most need it. | <a id="fjs-1050"></a>FJS-1050 | css — **The vocabulary's both-directions check exempts a term whose class is `null`, so a term with NEITHER an element nor a class is graded by nothing — which is how `Group` shipped no CSS for its whole life.** Found 2026-09-08 ruling [FJS-D252](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d252). `vocabClass` returns `row[3]` where the row has one and the lowercased term otherwise ([vocabulary.js:712](packages/css/vocabulary.js#L712)), and the forward test returns early on `t.cls === null` with the reason *carried by an element; nothing to find* ([vocabulary.spec.js:62](packages/css/test/specs/vocabulary.spec.js#L62)). **The exemption is correct for the case it was written for and wrong for the one beside it**: `Section` is `<section>` and needs no class, while `Group` was declared `<div>` — an element that conveys nothing — so *carried by an element* was false and the term could not be written at all. It was named in the vocabulary, routed by the decision wizard, and rendered nowhere. **The distinguishing fact is in the row already**: a `null` class beside a SEMANTIC element is a term the browser carries, and a `null` class beside `<div>` is a term with no way to exist. So the check can grade it — a `null` class is legitimate only where `element` is not a bare `<div>` — which is a condition rather than a new list, and the reason this is filed rather than left as a note. Fixed for Group by shipping `.group`; every other `null`-class term is ungraded until the condition lands | 2026-10-14 | The forward vocabulary check returned early on any null class, so a term with no class beside a bare <div> was graded by nothing. vocabulary.spec.js now fails a null-class term whose element is <div>; proved red by setting Text's element to <div> (1 failing), green on the real vocabulary (css suite 553 passing). Also corrected vocabulary.js header, which still called Group structural. · [vocabulary.spec.js](packages/css/test/specs/vocabulary.spec.js) · [vocabulary.js `vocabClass`](packages/css/vocabulary.js#L711) · [FJS-D252](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d252) |

| <a id="fjs-d908"></a>FJS-D908 | litestone — **How does a per-row zone (a column, possibly two relations away) reach a where: a lowered zone-aware operator, a materialized instant, or a framework-bound per-zone window?** | 2026-10-13 | Ruled [`FJS-D908`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d908): **A** — a zone-aware operator the client lowers: the caller states the wall-clock rule and the zone field (`{ startsAt: { localTime: { atOrBefore: '08:00', zone: 'inviteeTimeZone' } } }`); litestone selects the distinct zones present (`SELECT DISTINCT zone`, bounded and indexable), computes each zone's instant bound with `fromWall`/`partsIn`, and lowers to `(zone = ? AND startsAt <= ?) OR …`. SQL stays instant-only, so `FJS-D143` stands and the cost is one DISTINCT plus an index range per zone. The zone must be a column of the same row; a zone two relations away (`Shift → Employee → User`) needs a join the lowering does not do today, so that case stays open or is solved by A + a denormalized zone column. Adds an operator to `where`, `$checkWhere` and the directive table. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |

| <a id="fjs-1410"></a>FJS-1410 | junction · litestone — **A custom method's ANSWER has no declaration: a `methods:` entry takes `input` and `gate` and nothing for what comes back, and the client's `invoke()` answers `Promise<unknown>`, so a `type` in `db/schema.lite` can describe a method's payload and never its result.** **Measured** 2026-09-27 in *Portal, the search stressor*. Discovery drafted `type Hit { url, title, snippet?, provider }` for the thing the app serves most, a search result. `litestone types` emits `interface Hit` for both audiences, and nothing can point at it: `MethodDeclaration` is `{ method, input?, gate? }` ([service.ts](packages/junction/src/core/service.ts)), `ServiceTypes` maps `usages` to the `Usage` row, and `invoke()`/`call()` return `unknown`. By Phase 2 the declared type had **drifted from the served answer** (`provider` beside `providers: string[]`, `domain`, `score` and `rule`) and no check noticed, because no check connects them. The shape lives in TS in the app's `domain/search/merge.ts`, and the terminal reads `res.hits` untyped; the `web/` page will too. So the answer a Resource or `<Table>` would bind to has no seed-side owner. Wanted: `{ method, input, output: 'SearchResult' }`, reaching the client's typed call and the surface snapshot as `input` already does. Neighbour of [`FJS-706`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-706) `core-11` (`app.service('x')` is `Promise<unknown>` on the server), and of [`FJS-1254`](#fjs-1254) (a `type` reaches the browser registry and the UI realm cannot address it) | 2026-10-11 | A `methods:` entry had no word for its answer. Added `output: 'Type'` beside `input` (`collectMethodOutputs`, `Service._outputs`, `describe().outputs`, `SurfaceService.outputs`), reported in the surface snapshot as `**output**` and as the OpenAPI 200 body of the custom-method operation (`$ref`, or a titled `oneOf` for several).
