| <a id="fjs-266"></a>FJS-266 | repo — **The framework tells an app to run Biome and runs nothing itself.** `FJS-D32` adopted a linter and `@frontierjs/config` ships the rule set every scaffolded app extends, but this repo does not extend it — a framework that lints itself with nothing while telling its users to lint has two answers to one question, which is the shape Invariant 4 exists to prevent. It was not turned on because the number was measured first: Biome's `recommended` gives **7,249** findings on this tree, and the shipped curated set gives **~600**, of which 123 are `noUnusedImports` and 25 are `noGlobalIsNan`. That is a countable cleanup with a direction, not the taste argument `IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md` 1 was blocked on. Work: add the devDependency and a root `biome.json` extending the package, clear the findings, then add a `lint` phase to `scripts/ci.mjs` — in that order, since a phase added first is a phase everyone learns to skip. One unexplained finding to resolve on the way: **Biome cannot parse `packages/mesa/test/runtime.test.js`** | 2026-10-10 | The repo now lints itself: @biomejs/biome 2.5.8 is a root devDependency and a root biome.json extends @frontierjs/config (whose own biome.json became root:false, or Biome refuses two roots), excluding only what is vendored or specification (vendor, mockup, .jetty-cache, html, svelte). The measured number had drifted — 4,218 findings, 2,740 of them vendored bundles — and was cleared to zero by autofix (unused imports and variables, parseInt radix, hasOwn, Number.isNaN where the operand was already a number), hand edits (void returns, a catch parameter assigned, a duplicate key, dead private field) and 53 biome-ignore comments each carrying its reason. The shipped set gained four principled loosenings with README reasons: useIterableCallbackReturn skips forEach, noEmptyInterface and noImplicitAnyLet off, folder patterns without the trailing /** (peer range now >=2.2.0). The unexplained parse finding was a duplicate $$eachBlock import in mesa/test/runtime.test.js (and a stray CSS fragment in mesa/example/index.html). scripts/ci.mjs has a lint phase (biome lint --error-on-warnings, 2.6s, fast tier) that passes. Proved by the suites of config, toolbelt, css, mesa, sierra, junction, litestone, caravan, auth, conduit, mcp, orion, outpost, jetty, email-kit, ui, basecamp and vscode, and the example verify:offline/widget/jobs/cart/pay drives; autofix broke css's page-injected scripts and two sierra destructures, caught by those suites and reverted. · [packages/config/biome.json](packages/config/biome.json) · [IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md](IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md) |

| <a id="fjs-1838"></a>FJS-1838 | auth — **confirmTotp is a six-digit oracle: no attempt ceiling, no limiter bucket, and no trail entry when a code is refused** | 2026-10-10 | confirmTotp had no ceiling, no limiter and no trail entry: the service never called reauthenticate and the provider threw a bare ReauthenticationFailedError on every miss. The service now takes the shared reauthentication bucket first (429 at login's 10 / 15 min), and the provider counts misses per pending enrollment, writes totp.confirm.failed to the trail on each, and deletes the pending credential at loginChallengeAttempts so the next try is setupTotp, which asks for the password. The count is in memory, not a column: the only caller is a session already holding the account and the service limiter is process-local too. A type parameter on `createTestEnv` (and on `@frontierjs/testing`'s re-export) would let a test name the app's client and drop the cast; the first test every new app gets currently teaches `as any`. | 2026-10-10 | Cause: TestEnv's db, system, actingAs() and atLevel() were the hand-written LitestoneClient, whose every table is an unknown index signature, and createTestEnv took no type argument. The scaffolded api/test/access.test.ts drops both 'as any' casts: it references db/schema.d.ts, and an app with tests gets typecheck = 'bun run db:types && fli typecheck' so a clone has the file. Proved by litestone test/test-env-typed.test.ts (tsc over the generator's real output: registered, explicit, and unregistered-stays-unknown) and cli test/app-config.test.js; typecheck baselines unchanged (litestone 56, basecamp 12). | <a id="fjs-940"></a>FJS-940 | junction — **A key inside a `junction.config.js` section is still stashed and read by nothing, and the interfaces cannot be the list that would catch it.** [`FJS-939`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-939) closed the TOP-LEVEL half — a section nothing reads is refused by name at `start()`. A key one level down is not, so `middleware: { helmet: true, csrfs: true }` and `caravan: { pollIntervel: 1000 }` still merge silently. **Refusing them is not the same shape as refusing a section, and the reason is measured**: the TypeScript interfaces are erased at runtime AND have already drifted from what reads them — `basecamp` declares `middleware.cors.credentials`, which `JunctionMiddlewareConfig.cors` does not name and `applyConfiguredCors` reads and honours (the interface was corrected in `FJS-939`; the drift is the finding). So a nested check means hand-keeping a key list per section beside an interface nobody updates, which is the second origin `FJS-D199` exists to remove. **What would make it decidable is one owner per section for *what keys does this have***, read by the reader AND the check the way `JUNCTION_SECTIONS` now is — six sections, so six lists, and the subsystem that consumes each one is the only honest place for it. **Measured 2026-09-13**: [`FJS-D256`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d256) gave `middleware:` and `plugins:` that owner for what the FRAMEWORK declares — `loadConfig` maps each key one at a time and `test/config-surface.test.ts` grades both directions — but a caller's misspelled key in any section is still dropped in silence, which is this row | 2026-10-10 | A key inside a `junction.config.js` section was merged in silence because no list of a section's keys existed that the reader and the check shared. Per FJS-D483 each reader now owns its list: `MIDDLEWARE_CONFIG_KEYS` (which `loadConfig` loops over), `PLUGINS_CONFIG_KEYS` and `SERVICES_CONFIG_KEYS` in `config/index.ts`, and a plugin states `Plugin.configKeys` for the section of its name (caravan's `CARAVAN_CONFIG_KEYS`). `unknownKeys` is checked beside `unknownSections` in `applyConfigFile`, so one boot reports `csrfs` → `csrf` and `pollIntervel` → `pollInterval` by name. `JunctionCaravanConfig` had drifted from the reader (five keys missing) and is corrected. Proved by `test/authoring-keys.test.ts` (typo refused, correct spelling boots), `test/config-surface.test.ts` (list = interface), caravan's `junction-integration.test.ts` (list = keys the reader reads, junction refuses `pollIntervel`; red with `configKeys` stubbed), junction 2789 and caravan 333 green, `example verify:jobs` boots; example and basecamp configs load clean. `example verify` fails at FJS-1642 (open at HEAD); basecamp `verify` found :8120 held by another session. `app`, `attachments` and `conduit` stay unchecked (FJS-2483). · [config/index.ts](packages/junction/src/config/index.ts) · [FJS-939](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-939) · [FJS-D199](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d199) · [FJS-706](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-706) |

White space collapses as a browser's does, across tag edges and at a line's start, and the emitter now keeps the white space between two siblings that may share a line. A button is a flow too, so a label's edge spaces collapse into its brackets, and a field is 20 cells wide unless `size` says otherwise. `specs/flow.spec.mjs` 28/28, 16 deliberate breaks all red; drive 255. `/invoices/` reads as prose. A link stays a node of its own, so prose breaks at a link's edges: [`FJS-2326`](#fjs-2326) |
| <a id="fjs-2317"></a>FJS-2317 | litestone — **@@trail added 100–170 µs to every audited write, twenty times the create it records, because each entry paid its own index commit** | 2026-10-10 | Found by the 2026-10-09 performance audit (R5), whose diagnosis was half right. Split on this machine: building the entry is ~3 µs, the bare JSONL append ~14 µs, and the index's BEGIN IMMEDIATE + INSERT + COMMIT ~90–120 µs — five B-tree pages (the table and four indexes) into the WAL per line, plus the checkpoints they bring. The create pipeline the audit blamed is not the cost, so no raw append path was built. Fix: fireLog queues per log table, and the entries one tick produced go down as one createMany, so one lock and one commit; a lone write is still one create. A batch that throws is retried entry by entry, so one entry a SQL trail's own model refuses drops that entry and not the others, and $logStats counts per entry. A SQL trail's batch announces one collection event where single creates announced rows. Ablation create/log-audit: +168 µs to +25 µs at load ~10. That bench writes in one tick, so the gain is for a request or job writing several rows; a request writing one row still pays one commit. Proved by trail-batch.test.ts (one createMany per tick, lines in order with the index naming each, the refused-entry fallback); log-flush-on-exit.test.ts unchanged · [audit-log.js](packages/litestone/src/core/audit-log.js) · [trail-batch.test.ts](packages/litestone/test/trail-batch.test.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-2297"></a>FJS-2297 | litestone — **A scoped caller writing a @secret column through `system: [col]` files a trail entry saying the field went null to null, and both row images omit it, where the same write as system logs `[redacted]`** | 2026-10-10 | The trail's images were the row as the caller reads it: the update prefetch and the row a write read back both pass through read(), whose field policy strips a protected column for a non-system caller, so redaction never saw the column and a scoped system: ['apiKey'] write logged null to null with images missing it. trailImage() in makeTable overlays the column's [redacted] or [personal] mark wherever the stored row holds a value the caller's row lacks, and is applied to the update prefetch and to the row writeUnit hands finishWrite for the trail — update, create, delete, soft remove, upsert — never to the row the caller gets. The same overlay now gives an asSystem image of a @hashed column its mark, which read() strips for everyone. test/trail-scoped-redaction.test.ts: update, create and delete, as system and through system: [], red on the three scoped cases with the overlay stubbed. | <a id="fjs-2308"></a>FJS-2308 | litestone — **A caller can put another row's stored ref in a File[] on create, and replacing that array later deletes the other row's file from storage** | 2026-10-10 | FileStorage passed a File[] item that was not a file value straight through as a stored ref, so a create could store another row's key and the row's next replace or delete had the provider delete the other row's file. | <a id="fjs-2314"></a>FJS-2314 | litestone · sierra — **The OPFS pool VFS refuses `journal_mode = WAL` in silence, so every autocommit write on a device was a rollback-journal cycle: 10–12 ms a row in Chrome** | 2026-10-09 | Found by the 2026-10-09 performance audit (B1). The pool has no xShmMap, so the WAL pragma answers the previous mode and `synchronous = NORMAL` did nothing. Measured in Chrome over the pool, 300 autocommit inserts: DELETE/NORMAL 12.1 ms, PERSIST/NORMAL 6.3, PERSIST/OFF 0.113, MEMORY/OFF 0.063. Fix: an engine may declare `journal: { mode, synchronous }` (checked against SQLite's words in setEngine, since it is spliced into a PRAGMA); sqlite-wasm declares PERSIST/OFF, which keeps a journal that rolls back a killed tab — MEMORY would lose the file to one. Only a power loss mid-commit can cost the file, which is a cache (unsent writes live in IndexedDB). The wasm path no longer reaches applyWal, so its SharedArrayBuffer busy-retry cannot fire in a worker. Proved by the browser drive (new row: 30 single creates under 2.5 ms each, red at 10.1) and engine-seam.test.ts (a bad journal refused by name). · [sqlite-wasm.js](packages/litestone/src/engines/sqlite-wasm.js) · [databases.js](packages/litestone/src/core/databases.js) · [engine.js](packages/litestone/src/core/engine.js) |
| <a id="fjs-2313"></a>FJS-2313 | litestone — **Every non-system write ran one exists() per foreign key it named, whether or not the parent could hide anything, so a plain create naming two parents was three statements** | 2026-10-09 | Found by the 2026-10-09 performance audit (R2). Fix: hiddenParents asks the parent table `tbl[NARROWED]()` — READ_RULES' own `narrows`, the same answer FJS-2312 uses — and when no rule narrows it and the gate admits the model (beforeRead, no query), the parent cannot be hidden and no exists() runs. A gate refusal falls through to the existing two-query verdict. The audit's proposed skip list left out soft delete, templates and the effective window, which would have admitted a create under a soft-deleted parent; deriving from READ_RULES cannot drift that way. Proved by fast-paths.test.ts (no exists() for an open parent; red on HEAD) and hidden-parent.test.ts unchanged. · [client.js](packages/litestone/src/core/client.js) |
| <a id="fjs-2312"></a>FJS-2312 | litestone — **One @@gate or @@allow anywhere in a schema turned the findUnique-by-pk and findMany({}) fast paths off for every model, and every verb scanned every model's shape for a policied aggregate** | 2026-10-09 | Found by the 2026-10-09 performance audit (R3, R4). Both preconditions were client-wide (`ctx.hasPolicies`, `plugins.hasPlugins`), so in basecamp — every model gated — the paths were dead code. Fix: each READ_RULES row declares `narrows` (refused at load without one), and the fast paths run when no rule but soft delete narrows this model for this flavor, with the plugin beforeRead/afterRead hooks around the statement; a beforeRead that rewrites the args is honored by asking the shape again after it. buildSQL's own shortcut, which assumed the old preconditions, asks the same and only for a read verb. | <a id="fjs-d666"></a>FJS-D666 | litestone — **How does a JSON or /mcp caller supply a File column: an inline data-URL value FileStorage reads as bytes, an upload route whose ref the create then accepts, or both?** | 2026-10-10 | Ruled [`FJS-D666`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d666): **A** — an inline value: a data URL (RFC 2397, `data:<mime>;base64,…`) or `{ name, type, data }` with base64 `data`, which `readValue` decodes into bytes like a Buffer, `@accept` sniffing the bytes and not trusting the claimed type. The input schema for a File column is derived to describe that value rather than `FileRef`. The bound is junction's `http.maxBodySize`, the one a browser's multipart upload already meets, so it is not a new option. Its default is 256KB and base64 adds a third, so about 190KB of file gets through untouched: a phone photo (2–5MB) is refused until the app raises that setting, which is the same raise a form upload of that photo already needs. Today the 413 reads *Request body exceeds 262144 bytes* and names nothing to raise, so it names `http.maxBodySize`. One call, and the server stays the only author of a ref. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |

## See also

- `ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md` — closed rows aged out of § Closed. Same table, verbatim. Read when tracing a specific id, never cold.
- `CLAUDE.md` § Live hazards — traps that are **correct behavior**; knowing them saves a day. Not issues.
- `DECISIONS.md` — settled rulings. A `FJS-D##` closing here lands there.
- `IDEAS/` — roadmap and design records for work not started. `IDEAS/overview.md`'s wave 0 is the subset of this file that happens to be argued in an ideas file.
- `HANDOFF.md` — per-session narrative, newest first. History, not a ledger.
- `VERIFYING.md` — how to promote a `stale?` row to `open` or `closed`.
